vignette:
Patient: “Tama” (pseudonym), age 63, male, Oceania (Samoan descent), widowed, construction worker.

Tama begins each session by smoothing the crease of his jeans, a slow, deliberate motion that seems to ground him. He speaks in a low, measured voice, a voice used to calling out over the roar of jackhammers and cement mixers. For thirty-eight years, he has been a laborer on high-rise projects, a man known for his steady hands and his quiet reliability. But the scaffolding of his life, he tells me, has been rotten at the core for a long time.

The story starts in the kitchen of their small apartment, twenty-two years ago. He was forty-one, a foreman then, tired after a double shift. His wife, Leilani, was beautiful, fierce, and her anger was a sudden storm. That night, the argument was about nothing—a missed call, a late dinner. He remembers the flash of the ceramic bowl, the sharp crack against his temple, the warm trickle of blood. He remembers the shock, not the pain. He didn’t fight back. He never did. That was the rule he lived by: a man does not raise his hand to a woman. So he took it. He took the thrown plates, the shoves, the times she locked him out of the house in the rain. He took the silent treatment that could last for weeks, a punishment more chilling than any blow.

He tells me he never told anyone. Not his pastor, not his brothers on the crew. He was ashamed. A Samoan man, a provider, a protector—how could he admit he was afraid of his own wife? He learned to read her moods like a weather forecast: the tightening of her jaw meant a squall was coming. He would make himself small, invisible. He started working longer hours, volunteering for the dirtiest jobs, just to stay away.

Leilani died of cancer six years ago. He was her caregiver until the end. He never spoke of the past. He thought the story would die with her.

It didn’t.

Now, at sixty-three, his body is a chronicle of that old violence. He has a constant, dull ache in his lower back from a fall she pushed him down the stairs. His right shoulder seizes up when he reaches for a tool, a souvenir of a dislocated joint she wrenched. But it’s the hypervigilance that is destroying him on the job. Last month, a young apprentice dropped a steel beam near his foot. The sound was a flat, metallic clang. Tama’s body reacted before his mind could. He dropped to his knees, hands over his head, heart hammering against his ribs like a trapped bird. He stayed there, shaking, for ten minutes, while the crew stared. He told them he had a dizzy spell. He knows they don’t believe him.

The worst part is the silence. The crew’s silence. His silence. He comes home to an empty house that still smells like her jasmine perfume, a ghost he cannot exorcise. He cannot sleep. At night, he replays the arguments, the apologies he never received, the rage he swallowed. He has nightmares where she is not dead, but simply waiting for him in the dark living room, a shadow with a familiar, cruel smile. He wakes up gasping, his sheets soaked with sweat, his fists clenched. He has started drinking again, a few beers after work, just to blunt the edge of the memories.

The other day, a foreman yelled at him for a small mistake. The man was just loud, not threatening. But Tama felt his throat close up. He saw the man’s raised hand, and for a split second, it was Leilani’s hand. He flinched. A grown man, a veteran of the concrete jungle, flinching at a raised voice. The humiliation is a new kind of poison.

He tells me he is tired. Not from the work, but from the carrying. He says he feels like a condemned building, still standing but structurally unsound, waiting for one more tremor to bring it all down.
